messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Pharmacist
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Ethan's Story

Ethan Parata was twenty-four when his older brother Kai died. It happened on a Friday night in March, two years ago, though the specific sequence of events still refuses to arrange itself into a coherent narrative in Ethan's mind. He knows that Kai had been drinking at a friend's house. He knows that Kai drove. He knows that somewhere on the Pacific Coast Highway, Kai's car crossed the median. He knows his mother called him at midnight. Beyond those anchors, the story fragments—pieces that won't fit together, gaps he cannot fill even when he tries to reconstruct it deliberately. Sometimes he remembers the hospital waiting room; sometimes he remembers his father's face. But he cannot hold the whole thing in his mind at once, cannot tell it as a beginning, middle, and end. It is only a series of moments that happened to someone else, to a version of Ethan who no longer exists.

Kai had always been the golden one. Three years older, confident, the kind of person who made friends easily and seemed to know instinctively how to live. Ethan had followed him into pharmacy school—not because he wanted to, he realized later, but because Kai had made it seem possible, achievable, normal. In the weeks after Kai's death, Ethan found himself unable to sit in the pharmacy where he now worked without feeling the weight of that mimicry, that false inheritance of Kai's certainty. He had come to believe that his life was destroyed, that he had been following a path that was never truly his, that the person he had been before—the one who could laugh, who had felt purposeful in his work—had died along with Kai.

The smell of alcohol undoes him. It arrives without warning: a customer at the pharmacy who has been drinking, a colleague's breath, the sharp tang of hand sanitizer on a particularly bad day. His body reacts before his mind has time to register what is happening. His chest tightens. His hands shake. He becomes hypervigilant, scanning the pharmacy for danger that he knows, intellectually, is not there. He has come to understand that his body is constantly braced, as if waiting for another catastrophe, as if remaining vigilant enough might somehow prevent what has already happened. At night, he lies awake, muscles tense, certain that something terrible is about to occur, only to wake to the ordinary silence of his apartment.

Ethan has begun avoiding situations where he might encounter people behaving recklessly or selfishly. He stopped attending his weekly soccer league because of a player who had shown up late and dismissive of the team's rules. The violation—the disregard for others, the carelessness—triggered something in him that felt like rage and terror combined. He finds himself judging people harshly, withdrawing from friends who drink, creating distance from anyone whose behavior seems to him morally compromised. When he recalls Kai's decision to drive that night, the guilt is suffocating. Kai was reckless. Kai made a choice. And Ethan cannot separate his grief from his anger at that choice, cannot hold both feelings without feeling like he is betraying his brother.

When his mother invited him to a cemetery dedication last month—a small gathering to mark Kai's grave with a new stone—Ethan's body seized with panic before his mind could process the invitation. He could not go. The thought of standing in that space, surrounded by the physical reality of his brother's death, surrounded by his family's grief, felt impossible. He declined. His mother has not called since.

It is this avoidance, this shrinking away from the world, that finally brought Ethan to his first therapy appointment. He is twenty-six now, and he realizes that he has spent the last two years becoming smaller—smaller in his job, smaller in his relationships, smaller in his own life. He came seeking help not because he believes he can be fixed, but because he is afraid that if he continues as he is, there will be nothing left of him at all. What he fears most is that this is permanent, that the person he was before Kai died is truly gone. What he hopes for, though he barely dares to articulate it, is some way to live alongside the grief without being consumed by it.
